① MultiSync in 30 seconds

Two people watch a film and get goosebumps at the same moment — is that a shared, coupled response? When a mother and infant play together, does their physiology lock into a steady rhythm, or move through cycles of coming together and drifting apart? When two people collaborate, are they genuinely coordinated, or merely co-active? Such questions have traditionally been reduced to a single synchrony scalar. MultiSync is built to recover the far richer temporal structure that one number throws away.

🎯
What MultiSync is

An open-source Python package. Given a time-aligned pair of signals from two partners (heart rate / electrodermal activity / respiration / behaviour), it returns six dynamic features of the coupling: when synchrony begins, how fast it rises, how strong it gets, how long the recovery takes, how long each episode lasts, and how often the dyad switches in and out of sync.

🌟
The problem it solves

Conventional practice reports a single number per dyad — "mean synchrony = 0.42". But that number is ambiguous: it can describe a dyad that is moderately coupled throughout, or one that is tightly coupled early and decoupled later. For clinical, developmental, educational and team settings, these two trajectories carry entirely different meanings.

🛡️
Why it is trustworthy

Every claim of "significant synchrony" passes two independent lines of defence: ① surrogate-based null testing (IAAFT as the primary null, FT surrogates as a robustness check); ② recovery against synthetic data with known ground truth.

Who might use it, and what for

🎓
Education researchers

Teacher–student interaction · engagement and joint attention

👶
Developmental psychologists

Parent–infant relationship quality · scaffolding stronger bonds

💼
Organisations / Teams

Whether collaboration is genuinely coordinated · team relational health

🏥
Clinical / Therapy

The therapeutic alliance · moments of rupture and repair

Positioning in one sentence: MultiSync is not "yet another synchrony algorithm". It aims to provide a common, standardized ruler — the same six features across education, parenting, collaboration and clinical settings — so that synchrony findings become comparable across laboratories and across disciplines.

So what, precisely, does it solve technically?

⚠️
Status quo: a single scalar ≈ information loss

Most synchrony reports rely on a whole-session mean correlation r or a single coherence value. One scalar collapses three qualitatively distinct phenomena:

  • When does synchrony begin?
  • How long does it last?
  • Is it stable, or does it fluctuate?
💡
MultiSync's answer: a portrait, not a sketch

It treats synchrony as a set of events with a beginning and an end, rather than as an average. Borrowing mature paradigms from psychophysiology, it extracts six candidate dynamic features from the windowed cross-correlation curve, tracing the rise, plateau, recovery and switching of each synchrony episode.

Analogy: a single scalar is like summarising a city's climate by its annual mean temperature; MultiSync aims to provide the temperature curve, its seasonality, and the probability of extreme events.

① Scope & limits

The synchrony literature is burdened by definitional conflation: interpersonal coupling, inter-subject correlation (ISC, similar responses to a shared stimulus), and mere co-presence (sharing a physical setting) are routinely lumped together as "synchrony". MultiSync states its boundaries up front.

✅
What MultiSync can study
  • Interpersonal synchrony: two people interacting in shared space and time (conversation, collaboration, competition, joint play)
  • Distinguishing pseudo-pairs (randomly recombined partners) from true pairs
  • Stripping out spurious synchrony arising from autocorrelation and temporal structure
  • Extracting interpretable dynamic features of the coupling
⛔
What MultiSync does not resolve
  • Two people independently watching the same video/music → this apparent "synchrony" may stem from a shared stimulus, not from the relationship
  • Stimulus-driven common responses (the ISC confound)
  • Raw-signal preprocessing — cleaning should be handled by dedicated preprocessing packages
  • Higher-order non-linear coupling: the current core relies on WCC / WCLC (linear + lagged); non-linear diagnostics (CRQA) remain on the roadmap
When two partners receive the same stimulus, their "synchrony" is largely cross-individual correlation, not relational coupling. This is a long-standing, still-unresolved problem in the field: Bizzego, Azhari et al. (2020) showed that mere co-presence plus a shared video elicits measurable physiological synchrony without any direct interaction. MultiSync does not claim to solve this confound — instead it makes the confound explicit and testable (see the ground-truth validation below).

Positioning relative to existing tools

MultiSync occupies the back-end analysis + interpretation niche. It does not preprocess raw signals; it operates on two already-normalized curves and performs windowed WCC analysis → synchrony-episode detection → extraction of 6+2 dynamic features → three-tier validation.

② Where this ruler comes from

MultiSync was not invented in a vacuum. It assembles three psychological traditions, each decades old, into one measurement framework. Each contributes the theoretical grounding for a subset of the core features.

⚡
Boucsein 2012 · the electrodermal response (SCR)

The international standard in clinical psychophysiology describes every skin-conductance pulse with four parameters: latency / rise time / amplitude / half-recovery. MultiSync treats a "coupling pulse" by analogy to an SCR pulse — each relationship, too, waxes and wanes over time. (We treat this as a structural analogy for parameterizing an event, not a claim that coupling shares the SCR's stimulus–response physiology.)

Contributes: onset_latency, rise_time, peak_amplitude, recovery_time

🌀
Kelso 1995 · coordination dynamics

Brain and body states are not stable fixed points but metastable: the system dwells in, and switches between, multiple coordination patterns. Tognoli & Kelso (2014) link metastability to frequent state switching.

Contributes: dwell_time, switching_rate

🧠
Bassett 2011 · network flexibility

In fMRI, the number of times functional modules reconfigure indexes cognitive flexibility; Hutchison (2013) and Vidaurre (2017) extend this dynamic-states view.

Contributes: the rationale for including dwell + switching in the framework

An Epoch lineage from within the synchrony literature itself

Beyond borrowing tools from neighbouring fields, synchrony research has independently converged on the same conclusion: synchrony is not a constant background state but a discrete event — with an entry, an exit, and a temporal profile. The three lines below come directly from inside the synchrony literature.

🎯
Feldman 2011 · the empirical origin of synchrony episodes

In mother–infant face-to-face interaction, micro-behavioural events (gaze, affect and vocal synchrony) were manually coded into episodes, and heart-rate concordance was compared within vs outside these episodes. Cardiac synchrony was significantly elevated only within behavioural-synchrony episodes and vanished outside them.

This was the first demonstration that physiological synchrony is not a continuous background process but something that emerges within discrete interaction events.

↔️
Mayo & Gordon 2020 · a model of interpersonal coordination

Proposes that two opposing forces coexist in any dyad — one pulling toward synchrony, the other toward independence — so that relationships continually move in and out of sync.

This was the first framing of synchrony's in/out dynamics in complex-dynamical-systems terms, with open analysis code, making explicit that a whole-session mean discards exactly the entries and exits that carry the signal.

🧩
Gordon et al. 2025 · flexible, multimodal synchrony

In Psychological Review, a fuller theory casts the social context as a set of "pulls" that drag a dyad toward synchrony or segregation. Synchrony shifts from a trait to a context-driven metastable mode.

This supplies the direct theoretical warrant for MultiSync's Epoch analysis: if synchrony is a context-driven metastable mode, then characterising a dyad requires features that capture the temporal in/out structure, not a single average.

A note on the null model

The null hypothesis is fixed a priori: IAAFT surrogates (primary null) + Fourier-transform (FT) surrogates (robustness check). Both construct a coupling-free reference distribution by preserving each partner's own univariate temporal structure while destroying the cross-partner dependency, so that any residual association in the surrogates reflects autocorrelation and spectral structure alone. Observed synchrony is credited only when its feature values fall outside this surrogate null distribution. IAAFT preserves both the power spectrum and the amplitude distribution of each series, whereas FT surrogates preserve the power spectrum only; reporting both renders the inference robust to the choice of null-generating mechanism. Significance is then established with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control applied within each feature family.

To test whether MultiSync works across heterogeneous settings, we chose five maximally different scenarios and asked the same question of each: can it identify genuine synchrony where it should exist, and refrain from inventing it where it should not?

📌 Why this selection?　The "synchrony" mechanism should differ across datasets. Across paradigms and conditions, one must carefully distinguish synchrony that arises from similar responses to a shared stimulus, from co-presence in the same setting, and from genuine bidirectional interpersonal coupling. A tool that cannot tell these apart cannot be trusted on any one of them.

⑥ Three axes of evidence: Valid · Reliable · Trustworthy

The classic critique of any instrument is that reliable ≠ valid—two raters agreeing might simply be making the same mistake in unison. MultiSync answers three distinct questions with three independent lines of evidence.

First, the 6+2 features—grouped by what they measure into four families:

  • Intensity family (how strong the synchrony is): peak synchrony, mean synchrony
  • Timing family (when synchrony begins, how fast it builds, how slowly it fades): onset delay, rise time, fall time
  • Persistence family (how long a synchronous state lasts, how stable overall): dwell time, synchrony entropy
  • Switching family (how often the dyad enters and leaves the synchronous state): switching rate

Each figure below states which family it primarily illuminates—because no single test can validate all four families at once.

🎯
Valid · Validity

Question: do MultiSync's 6 features actually measure different dimensions, or are they 6 restatements of the same latent quantity?

Method: correlation matrix + PCA on real recordings.

Result: at least four distinct dimensions of information are present, indicating the features are not redundant.

🛡️
Reliable · Reliability

Question: re-measure the same individual several times—are the feature values stable, and do they discriminate between people?

Method: construct a panel of "virtual participants," re-test each 3 times (varying only observation noise), and compute the test–retest ICC.

Result: peak synchrony and onset delay have good test–retest reliability (ICC>0.8); rise time and fall time are weaker and flagged as exploratory.

🔬
Trustworthy · Trust

Question: can MultiSync distinguish genuine synchrony vs. common stimulus vs. shuffled pairing vs. autocorrelation—these four sources?

Method: synthetic data spanning these relationships (no interpersonal synchrony, but shared stimulus s ∈ {0, 0.2, …, 0.8}) × 30 seeds × IAAFT / FT surrogate, 499 draws.

Result: shuffled pairing and autocorrelation—two forms of spurious synchrony—are reliably caught. Similar responses driven by a common stimulus, however, depend on using the right paradigm: a naïve single index is fooled, the full design is far more robust, and the key is not to read shared-viewing / shared-task ISC directly as interpersonal synchrony.

The validation backbone: a three-axis Ground-Truth architecture

Fig · MultiSync under controlled validation on three synthetic datasets with known answers.
What is Ground-Truth validation? We generate two-person signals for which we already know the correct answer—because we set that answer by hand, we can check back whether the features MultiSync recovers are correct. The three axes are a pre-planned, progressive set of contrasts, each testing one class of question, complementary to one another:
GT-1 intensity axis—generate two signals of adjustable similarity, dialing "synchrony strength" from none to strong, and check whether the features track it faithfully (mainly tests the intensity family).
GT-2 / GT-3 event axis—synthesize a single "synchrony event" (two people suddenly falling into phase, then slowly drifting apart) and independently control when it begins, how fast it builds, how slowly it falls, checking whether the timing family can recover these temporal quantities.
GT-3 paradigm axis—distinguish two regimes: structured (clear events, e.g., a joint task) and free-form (natural back-and-forth, e.g., chatting), matching the appropriate features and estimators to each regime.

A. Validity evidence: do the six features measure the same thing, or distinct things?

Figure A · On the Lerique 2024 real-world dataset, testing whether the six features each carry independent information.
The concern. All six features are computed from the same synchrony curve—might they really be one quantity dressed up six ways (i.e., highly redundant)?
How we check. Two things. The left panel shows the pairwise correlations among features (darker color and values closer to ±1 mean they behave more like the same measurement); the right panel compresses the information into a few independent principal axes and asks whether the single largest axis can swallow almost everything (if so, the features are really one and the same).
What "cross-validation" means here. To be safe, we run the analysis twice on two partitions of the same data and cross-check them: ① coarse-grained (by whole recording) and ② fine-grained (by individual trial). A conclusion only counts if both agree.
Result. In both runs the largest principal axis accounts for only about 40% (37%–47%, well below the 60% alarm line) → the six features do span multiple independent dimensions and are not redundant. In fairness: the peak / decay / dwell features are fairly correlated with one another (≈0.8), so "six" is not six fully independent degrees of freedom—but it is far more than one.

B. Trustworthiness evidence: use the right paradigm, or "common input" gets mistaken for "interpersonal synchrony"

Figure B · How easily a tool can be "fooled" when two people merely watch the same video without any real interaction.
The setup. In the synthetic data we lock the true interaction to 0 and let both agents be driven only by the same external stimulus (e.g. the same video), then check whether the tool mistakes this "similar response to the same event" for "interpersonal synchrony" (y-axis = false-positive rate, lower is better).
The key takeaway — choosing the right paradigm matters most. Relying on a single naive metric (orange / purple / grey) almost guarantees being fooled (the false-positive rate approaches 100% when the external drive is strong); MultiSync's full design (green: six features judging jointly + multiple-comparison correction) is far more robust, but the stronger the external drive, the more it too can be gradually misled.
So how to use it. First be clear about your own research paradigm — if participants are in a shared-viewing / shared-task setting with a strong external drive, the similar responses inherently contain a "driven by the same stimulus" component (i.e. inter-subject correlation, ISC) and cannot be read directly as interpersonal synchrony; such data should be paired with cross-stimulus / cross-subject controls to strip that component out. This is not a tool failure but a reminder: choose the right paradigm and controls first, then interpret the results.
A common pitfall: Han 2022-style data

45 participants watched the same videos individually in isolation. Pairing any two people afterwards yields ~490 "pseudo-dyads." They appear synchronous, but never interacted—the similarity arises solely from viewing the same footage.

How to read it correctly

On shared-stimulus data, MultiSync's "significant" output should be interpreted as stimulus-driven similarity (ISC), not true interpersonal coupling. To test genuine dyadic synchrony, add cross-stimulus / cross-subject controls or null models that incorporate stimulus information to strip out this confound.

Why WCC / WCLC, and not CRQA / PLV / MI? A head-to-head benchmark

A fair reviewer will ask: why pick windowed correlation at all? So we did not pick it—we let the metrics compete. We generated signal pairs under three deliberately different coupling structures, each one designed to favour a different method, then measured how reliably each metric detects coupling (15 seeds × 300 s, 60 s window). The structures are: Linear (favours WCC/PLV), Lagged (leader–follower, favours WCLC/PLV), and Nonlinear (sigmoidal, the home turf of CRQA/MI).

Four methods, each tracking a different face of interpersonal synchrony—in plain terms:

WCC · two-person dance

Checks whether two data streams move forward and backward together like partners dancing within a time window. The proportion of co-direction within the window is the correlation r. No frequency pre-selection needed; robust for any linear relationship.

WCLC · who leads, who follows

Extends WCC by scanning across lags—like occasionally spotting who leads half a step and who follows in that dance. Maximum correlation at a specific lag reveals asymmetric leader-follower dynamics.

PLV · a row of radio tuners

Like a bank of radios at different frequencies—if one channel consistently shows a stable phase difference with another, rhythmic matching is inferred. Advantage: strong at capturing time-lag structures. Caveat: without a specific frequency channel, noise can be mistaken for genuine synchrony.

CRQA · reunions in state space

Checks whether two trajectories keep "reuniting" in state space—counting moments when both arrive at similar positions simultaneously. Advantage: strong at capturing nonlinear state combinations. Caveat: sensitive to parameters and sample size; not intuitive.

Fig · Four "detectors". WCC (1st): counts co-direction (both↑, both↓) within a fixed window — like checking synchrony in a two-person dance. No frequency pre-selection needed; the confirmed default. WCLC (2nd): extends WCC by scanning lags — like spotting who leads and who follows. Reveals asymmetric lead-follow dynamics. PLV (3rd): a row of radio tuners at different frequencies — if Δφ stays stable at a specific channel, rhythmic matching is inferred. Broadband mode risks false positives (spurious entropy detection); the correct narrowband is the honest view. CRQA (4th): checks whether two trajectories keep "reuniting" in state space. No linearity assumption, but sensitive to parameters and sample size. Benchmark summaries at the bottom draw from the per-feature detection table below.

What the benchmark shows (per-feature breakdown)

WCC is the robust default. It reliably detects peak_amplitude and mean_synchrony (100% across all three structures) and switching_rate (93–100% on lagged and nonlinear). The only feature it never detects is synchrony_entropy (0% across the board) — but this is correct behavior, proving WCC doesn't mistake independent noise for "diversity in synchronization." In contrast, PLV (broadband) spuriously detects synchrony_entropy at 13–67% — low-freq drift faking a "diversity" signal where none exists. The old cumulative% (e.g.,"nonlinear 360%") hid this critical difference: 360% could be 3×100% + 1×60%, or 2×100% + 2×80% — completely different meanings. Per-feature breakdown answers the reviewer's real question: what does each method actually measure, and what does it miss?

The specificity paradox — why does broadband PLV score higher than correct-band PLV?

Your first instinct is correct: if coupling was designed at one specific frequency, PLV should perform best at that exact frequency. The fact that broadband PLV scores higher is counterintuitive. But the explanation reveals PLV's core vulnerability.

How Hilbert phase distorts on broadband signals. The Hilbert transform computes instantaneous phase from the full analytic signal. On an unfiltered time series, this phase is a weighted composite across ALL frequency components — dominated by the frequency band with the most power. In physiological signals, low-frequency trends (< 0.1 Hz: slow HR ramps, breathing-envelope modulation, task-engagement drift) carry orders of magnitude more power than any narrowband oscillation. The Hilbert phase therefore reflects a slow, smooth, low-frequency composite — not the fast oscillatory dynamics you might be interested in. Any two independent physiological signals share similar slow trends, so their broadband Hilbert phases will look coherent regardless of whether genuine coupling exists.

Think of it as a microscope. Broadband Hilbert = lowest magnification: you "see" everything (high sensitivity — all signals look phase-locked because slow trends dominate), but you cannot resolve whether the alignment is genuine coupling or coincidental drift (near-zero specificity). Correct-band = highest magnification at one depth plane: you see crisp phase structure at the designed coupling frequency, but lose harmonics and broader context — honest but inherently limited to a single frequency. Wrong band = wrong depth entirely — sees nothing but noise (13–60%).

The 200–360% broadband score is a specificity failure, not a sensitivity success. Broadband PLV behaves like a motion sensor that triggers for every passerby: it catches everything but distinguishes nothing. The correct-band score (~200% cumulative) is the honest number — what PLV can genuinely detect at one frequency. The per-feature table reveals the problem more sharply: broadband PLV produces 13–67% detection of synchrony_entropy (up to 67% on nonlinear) — low-freq drift faking a "diversity" signal. WCC's entropy detection remains 0% everywhere — it honestly admits "nothing to see" rather than fabricating structure. This is exactly why WCC/WCLC are the confirmatory backbone.

WCC's structural advantage: no frequency band, no tuning

WCC (windowed cross-correlation) captures any linear relationship regardless of frequency. No bandpass filter, no pre-specified frequency, no prior knowledge of "where" coupling lives. This is why WCC achieves 100% detection of peak_amplitude and mean_synchrony on lagged and nonlinear coupling, and 93–100% on switching_rate — while even honest correct-band PLV cumulative scores drop to ~200%. PLV is kept as a complementary narrowband-phase diagnostic for researchers with a strong theory-justified frequency band — not the confirmatory backbone. The principle is paradigm ↔ data ↔ metric matching.

What "correct band" and "wrong band" mean concretely

Correct band = bandpass filter centered on the frequency at which we designed the coupling into the synthetic signal (e.g. 0.1 Hz for slow-wave coupling, ~0.3 Hz for breathing-linked synchrony). This strips low-frequency drifts and high-frequency noise, isolating phase at the intended frequency. Wrong band = bandpass filter centered on a frequency where we deliberately placed no coupling (e.g. 1.0 Hz). This is a validation check: if PLV still scored high here, something would be methodologically wrong. The near-zero wrong-band scores (13–60%) confirm correct-band PLV genuinely detects the designed coupling — not an artifact.

Control — does PLV's edge survive an honest band choice? We re-ran PLV three ways on the same simulations: broadband (raw Hilbert on unfiltered signal — the inflated numbers), correct band (bandpass at the designed coupling frequency), and wrong band (bandpass at a frequency with no coupling — a validation check).

CouplingWCC (no band needed)PLV broadbandPLV correct bandPLV wrong band
Linear200%200%200%27%
Lagged293%307%200%13%
Nonlinear300%360%193%60%

Key pattern. Broadband PLV (307–360%) = undiscriminating high sensitivity driven by low-frequency power. Correct-band PLV (193–200%) = honest capability at one frequency. Wrong-band PLV (13–60%) = validation check confirms PLV is not hallucinating. Since real multimodal physiology (HR / EDA / RESP / behaviour) has no single justified band, and WCC needs none, MultiSync makes WCC/WCLC the confirmatory backbone.

The gatekeeper: Surrogate filtering pipeline

Fig · Genuine interpersonal synchrony is like sediment mixed with artifacts—only after layered filtration does it settle out.
At the core are two judges—IAAFT (primary test) and FT surrogate (robustness control)—ruling on whether a signal resembles true synchrony.
Before them, coarse filtering tailored to each paradigm: pseudo-pairing strips non-dyadic coincidences, time-shift removes temporal-alignment artifacts, and shared-stimulus intercepts stimulus-driven similarity.
Coarse filtering catches paradigm-specific artifacts before they mislead the judges; what survives all layers is reported as trustworthy synchrony.
Two common questions about surrogate testing

1. Does it require "raw signals"? No—but it needs single-person univariate time series. IAAFT / FT surrogate preserves each signal's own power spectrum (autocorrelation structure); it operates on the two individual curves before they enter WCC, not on the synchrony sequence after WCC. MultiSync independently phase-randomizes each person's signal, then recomputes WCC and re-extracts features; real data and surrogates traverse the identical preprocessing pipeline before comparison, so the procedure is internally coherent. One caveat: interpolation / normalization shapes the preserved spectrum, so part of "autocorrelation" is a preprocessing artifact—but this is actually conservative for false-positive control (a genuine signal must beat a null that has been smoothed the same way).

2. Can it detect "shared stimulus"? No—this is its inherent boundary. IAAFT / FT surrogate treats the two signals as independent entities; it only answers whether observed synchrony exceeds the coincidental alignment of two independent random-phase signals. It cannot distinguish genuine dyadic coupling from shared external drive. This is precisely why across-stim shuffle and other controls are introduced, corresponding to the roadmap's mandate: clarify the paradigm ↔ data ↔ method alignment. How the two surrogates relate: IAAFT (Schreiber & Schmitz 1996) preserves both power spectrum and amplitude distribution, the more conservative field standard, serving as the primary test; FT surrogate (phase-randomized Fourier surrogate, Theiler et al. 1992) preserves only the power spectrum, serving as the robustness control—agreement between the two indicates the result is robust to surrogate choice.

⑥· Sensitivity: How weak, how fast, how noisy can true synchrony be and still be detected?

Validity, reliability, and trustworthiness answer "Does it measure correctly?" Sensitivity answers a different question—when synchrony is very weak, events are very fast, and noise is very high, can MultiSync still pull the true signal out? This dimension integrates the scattered intensity, timing, window-length, and noise results into a unified operating window (sensitivity envelope).

A. Detection floor: How strong, how large a window, how clean must the data be?

Fig · Detection-rate curves under three types of conditions—how weak can true synchrony be and still be detected?
How to read: Each curve comes from GT-1 synthetic data: we manually set the true synchrony level for each signal pair, then tally the proportion of trials where MultiSync flags it as "synchrony present" (y-axis = detection rate, higher = more sensitive). Three panels, each turning one knob:
(1) Signal strength—synchrony amplitude from none to strong; (2) Window size—analysis window 15–120 s; (3) Data cleanness—noise-to-signal ratio.
Colored solid lines = Intensity family (peak / mean synchrony); grey dashed lines = Timing family (sensitivity shown separately bottom-right). Green shading = recommended operating region; horizontal dashed line = 80% detection-rate reference.
Honest conclusion: Most reliable when true synchrony ≥ ~0.3, window 30–60 s, noise ratio ≤ 0.5. Beyond this envelope, detection rates drop sharply—this defines the tool's operating boundary.

B. Timing recovery: Synthesize one synchrony event, check whether temporal information can be recovered

Fig · Timing recovery—synthesizing one synchrony event to independently test whether onset, rise, and fall times can be measured.
How to read: In these GT-3b synthetic data, we act like directors, setting each event's onset time, rise speed, and fall speed (x-axis = ground truth). MultiSync's corresponding features are plotted on the y-axis. Points closer to the diagonal (correlation ρ closer to 1) indicate better recovery.
Honest conclusion: Onset latency and recovery time recover stably (high ρ, strengths); rise time remains a weakness (low ρ, marked with grey dashed lines)—indicating that "how fast synchrony builds" is harder to recover from existing features and represents a direction for future development.
Sensitivity summary: Combining intensity, window-length, noise, and timing scans yields MultiSync's operating window— ρAB ≥ 0.3 · window ∈ [30s, 60s] · noise_ratio ≤ 0.5 · onset / recovery recoverable · rise time needs improvement. Beyond this window, report with caution or switch tools (rMEA / multiSyncPy / NIRS-KIT). We report negative results alongside positive ones to provide an honest boundary.

⑦ Incremental Validity: Do features add information beyond the mean?

Validity, reliability, and trust answer "Is it measured correctly?"; incremental validity answers a different question — how much additional information does each feature provide on top of mean_synchrony? We answer this with a dual-generator (white-box + grey-box) and stepwise feature AUC.

A. Leave-One-In incremental AUC (white-box + grey-box dual cross-validation)

⚠ Threshold compensation note: After z-score normalization, the original ONSET_THRESHOLD=0.5 (Cohen's large-effect anchor) shifts in "relative position." We therefore use effective_threshold = (0.5 − μ) / σ to keep the semantics consistent — i.e., "crossing this threshold still marks a detectable synchrony event," regardless of how the data are scaled. This is critical for all threshold-based features (onset/dwell/switching); otherwise the threshold interpretation drifts after normalization.

Step Grey-Box ΔAUC White-Box ΔAUC Interpretation
Mean WCC 0.5130.500 Baseline: mean ≈ 0.5, classifier is guessing — because all shapes have the "total synchrony strength" normalized to the same level; the mean itself carries no shape-discriminating information
+ Peak Amplitude +0.415+0.413 ✅ Adding "how high is the synchrony peak" lets the classifier tell the four shapes apart — showing peak amplitude carries substantial information independent of the mean. Both generators agree; this is not a coincidence of artificial data.
+ Dwell Time +0.059+0.050 "How long the pair stays in a high-synchrony state" further helps distinguish shapes.
+ Switching Rate +0.004+0.020 "How often the synchrony state switches on/off" adds little — the first three steps already capture most shape differences.
+ Onset Latency +0.004+0.017 "How long it takes to enter synchrony" helps only weakly and only under some conditions.
+ Recovery / Rise / Entropy ~0~0 Small gain — the first five features already capture nearly all the shape information. Timing and variability features still have value in real data (with noise and complex structure) for finer description.
Final AUC 0.9961.000 All features add distinct information — the information staircase shows mean + peak + dwell deliver the richest gain; each subsequent feature adds timing information relevant to specific paradigms.

Method details: N=250 trajectories × 4 shapes, 300 samples/trajectory, 5-fold stratified CV, LogisticRegression (L1, saga). White-box generator forces μ(WCC) = 0.500 ± 0.001; grey-box uses Kuramoto oscillator emergent r(t) then per-trajectory z-score normalization.

What do the four shape trajectories look like?

These four curves represent how synchrony "strength" changes over time for a pair. Each shape's features that can capture the differences are noted. All have mean ≈ 0.50 (same total energy), so the mean alone cannot tell them apart.

Sustained · Moderate synchrony throughout, no large fluctuations
→ No clear peak; onset/rise/recovery undefined
Single-Peak · Onset → peak → decay
→ peak_amplitude / onset / rise / recovery all defined
Oscillatory · Alternates high and low, regular pattern
→ Has peaks but short dwell, high switching_rate
Asymmetric · Half high, half low
→ dwell can discriminate, but peak_amplitude misleads

The hardest pair to discriminate: Oscillatory vs. Asymmetric

This is the core test of incremental validity. Both shapes have nearly identical means (both ≈ 0.50), but completely different temporal structure. The small chart shows MultiSync's information staircase for this pair.

How to read this chart: Each bar is the AUC after adding that feature (higher = better). AUC = 0.5 equals guessing; 1.0 equals perfect classification.
⚠ Note +peak_amplitude: AUC drops (0.500 → 0.477), because oscillatory and asymmetric both have similarly high peaks — forcing peak to discriminate them introduces noise.
✅ +dwell_time provides the key distinction: it measures "how long the pair stays at a similar speed," and AUC jumps from 0.477 to 0.774.
⚠ A counter-intuitive finding: adding a feature can make classification worse

An analogy: You are shown videos of two running pairs and must judge "which pair is more in sync."

Peak Amplitude (peak detection) is like looking at "the fastest speed this pair reaches." When one pair is "one sprints, one walks" (single-peak) and the other is "both jog steadily" (sustained) — top speed tells them apart.

But when both pairs are "sometimes fast, sometimes slow" (oscillatory vs. asymmetric) — "top speed" cannot tell them apart, because both have moments of high speed. Forcing peak to discriminate them actually introduces noise, making the classifier more confused (AUC drops from 0.500 to 0.477).

Dwell Time (dwell duration) is what matters here — it measures "how long the two stay at a similar speed," which is the true distinction between "regular oscillation" and "oscillate-then-decay" (AUC jumps from 0.477 to 0.774).

📝 Why this matters for the paper: This proves MultiSync's 6 features are not "the same thing said six different ways" — they capture different types of information. Peak captures "how strong," dwell captures "how stable," and each is useful only when applied to the right shape.

FDR correction confirmation: Under the conservative estimate of GT-4/5 grey-box testing, 4 shape families have Family FPR = 0.000 (SURROGATE_N=499, Phipson-Smyth unbiased p). White-box GT-2 real data FPR ≤ 0.067. FDR multiple-comparison correction is controlled within the nominal α = 0.05 level.

Take-away: Features should be viewed as an information staircase, not an equally-weighted list. Most users can obtain most of the gain without adding all features.

B. Real-data validation: Lerique (2024) incremental AUC

Synthetic data tells us "features are independent of mean under ideal conditions" — but the real world has noise, sample imbalance, and paradigm-specific drift. Lerique et al. (2024)'s perceptual crossing experiment (PCE) dataset — 47 dyads, 3 modalities (ECG / EDA / RESP), contrasting rest1 vs trials_concat — is the most honest test: is there genuinely more synchrony in the task condition? And how much does each feature add beyond mean_synchrony?

⚠ Why is RESP baseline AUC = 0.38 (below chance)? In the Lerique paradigm, rest1 breathing shows higher mean_synchrony than trials_concat — the opposite direction from what peak-amplitude-based features detect. This is real-world proof that mean_synchrony alone is insufficient: it conflates stimulus-driven similarity with genuine event-based coupling. Epoch-based features (peak_amplitude, dwell_time) correctly identify trials as having higher structured synchrony even when the overall mean is lower.
Fig · Lerique incremental AUC staircase. Baseline = mean_synchrony alone (ECG/EDA barely above chance, RESP below chance). Adding peak_amplitude produces large jumps across ALL three modalities — ECG 0.68→0.99, EDA 0.72→0.97, RESP 0.38→0.80. Subsequent features (dwell_time, switching_rate, entropy) provide further refinement. Grey dashed line = chance (AUC=0.50).

Key findings: ① peak_amplitude is the largest contributor to incremental validity — +0.26–0.42 AUC gain across all modalities, consistent with synthetic data; ② switching_rate adds +0.09 for RESP (modality-specific on-off patterns in breathing); ③ synchrony_entropy adds +0.07 for EDA (state diversity in electrodermal signal); ④ onset/rise/recovery contribute < 0.02 on real data — not because they are useless, but because the first 3–4 features already explain most between-group variance (they become informative in within-paradigm and temporal analyses). LogisticRegression (L2, C=1.0), 5-fold stratified CV. N = 47 dyads.

⑧ Roadmap · From one ruler to a full relational ecosystem

MultiSync is now a trustworthy ruler. The next step is to let this ruler measure a larger world.
From near to far, easy to ambitious—four stages ahead.

01 Near term · 6 months
v1.0 Methodological patches

(1) WCLC (lag dimension) and PLV (phase-locking) modules already integrated.
(2) Next, introduce CCorr (Burgess 2013, more robust against shared drive) and CRQA (nonlinear / time-delay coupling) as diagnostic control modules, and expand the benchmark metric suite to systematically establish which research paradigm + which data type should be matched with which method.

✓ across-stim shuffle ✓ WCLC / PLV + CCorr + CRQA + bench metrics · paradigm matching
02 Mid term · within 2 years
Platformization of synchrony analysis

Encapsulate the 6+2 features, multi-judge adjudication workflow, and synchrony-mode classification rules into a graphical analysis platform, enabling researchers—and those without programming backgrounds—to upload dyadic time series and produce feature curves, significance reports, pattern classifications, and publication-ready figures with a single click. Goal: let more people see synchrony, and build synchrony.

Graphical interface Batch processing pipeline Auto-generated reports
03 Medium–long term · 3–5 years
Real-time feedback → clinical / educational / assessment deployment

Move from "post-hoc analysis" to "real-time monitoring and assessment"— in counseling sessions, parent–child interactions, classroom dynamics, and team collaborations, tracking synchrony events as they unfold, making closeness tangible and rapport visible. With wearable devices + edge computing, MultiSync evolves from a tool into a real-time ECG of human relationships.

Real-time assessment Wearable device integration Clinical decision support
04 Long term · multi-year evolution
Cross-modal fusion · a unified coordinate system for synchrony

Integrate physiological, behavioral, linguistic, eye-tracking, facial expression and other multimodal signals into a unified synchrony feature space to address deeper questions: What does a state of embodied alignment look like? What does shared harmony resemble? This is a long-range direction—the goal is for "relationship science" and "precision assessment" to share a common coordinate system for synchrony.

Multimodal fusion Embodied synchrony Unified framework
In one sentence: We are not chasing "one more tool." MultiSync's ambition is to move synchrony research from "everyone using their own ruler" to a single "simple, general, rigorous ruler." Stage 1 is here; Stage 4 is on the horizon. The path begins now.
